title: Chapter 45 — The Affidavit
paragraphs: As far as this book may have a narrative — and also because it indirectly touches on one or two very interesting and curious details of the habits of sperm whales — the foregoing chapter, in its earlier part, is as important as any to be found in this volume. But its leading matter needs to be enlarged upon still further, and more familiarly, in order to be properly understood, and also to remove any disbelief that a profound ignorance of the entire subject may produce in some minds as to the natural truth of the main points of this affair.

I do not care to do this part methodically, but will be content to make my point through separate examples of things practically or reliably known to me as a whaleman. From these examples, I trust, the conclusion I aim at will follow naturally.

First: I have personally known three instances where a whale, after receiving a harpoon, has made a complete escape and, after an interval (in one instance of three years), has been struck again by the same hand and killed — when the two irons, both marked with the same private cipher, have been taken from the body. In the instance where three years passed between the throwing of the two harpoons (and I think it may have been something more than that), the man who threw them happened in the interval to go in a trading ship on a voyage to Africa. He went ashore there, joined a discovery party, and made his way far into the interior, where he traveled for nearly two years, often endangered by serpents, savages, tigers, poisonous miasmas, and all the other common perils of wandering in the heart of unknown regions. Meanwhile the whale he had struck must also have been on its travels; no doubt it had circled the globe three times, brushing all the coasts of Africa with its flanks; but to no purpose. This man and this whale came together again, and the one vanquished the other. I say that I myself have known three instances like this: that is, in two of them I saw the whales struck, and after the second attack saw the two irons, with their respective marks cut in them, afterwards taken from the dead fish. In the three-year instance, it so happened that I was in the boat both times, first and last, and the last time I clearly recognized a peculiar sort of huge mole under the whale's eye which I had observed there three years before. I say three years, but I am pretty sure it was more than that. Here, then, are three instances whose truth I personally know; but I have heard of many other instances from people whose truthfulness in the matter there is no good reason to doubt.

Second: It is well known in the Sperm Whale Fishery, however ignorant the world ashore may be of it, that there have been several memorable historical cases where a particular whale in the ocean has been popularly recognizable at distant times and places. Why such a whale became marked in this way was not, entirely and originally, owing to bodily peculiarities distinguishing him from other whales; for however peculiar in that respect any chance whale may be, they soon put an end to his peculiarities by killing him and boiling him down into a peculiarly valuable oil. No: the reason was this — from the fatal experiences of the fishery, there hung about such a whale a terrible reputation for danger, as there did about the bandit Rinaldo Rinaldini, so much so that most fishermen were content to acknowledge him merely by touching their tarpaulin hats when they found him lounging near them on the sea, without trying to cultivate a closer acquaintance. Like some poor devils ashore who happen to know an irascible great man, they make distant, unobtrusive greetings to him in the street, for fear that if they pushed the acquaintance further they might get a summary thump for their presumption.

But each of these famous whales did more than enjoy great personal celebrity — no, call it ocean-wide renown; each was not only famous in life and immortal after death in forecastle stories, but was granted all the rights, privileges, and distinctions of a name, and had just as much of a name as Cambyses or Caesar. Wasn't it so, O Timor Tom! you famous leviathan, scarred like an iceberg, who lurked so long in the Oriental straits of that name, whose spout was often seen from the palm-lined beach of Ombay? Wasn't it so, O New Zealand Jack! you terror of all the cruisers that crossed their wakes near the Tattoo Land? Wasn't it so, O Morquan! King of Japan, whose tall jet, they say, sometimes took the shape of a snow-white cross against the sky? Wasn't it so, O Don Miguel! you Chilean whale, marked like an old tortoise with mystic hieroglyphics on your back! In plain prose, here are four whales as well known to students of Cetacean History as Marius or Sylla to the classical scholar.

But this is not all. New Zealand Tom and Don Miguel, after at various times causing great havoc among the boats of different ships, were finally hunted down, systematically pursued, and killed by valiant whaling captains who raised their anchors with that express purpose in mind — just as Captain Butler of old set out through the Narragansett Woods specifically to capture that notorious, murderous savage Annawon, the foremost warrior of the Indian King Philip.

I do not know where I can find a better place than right here to mention one or two other things which seem important to me, since in printed form they establish in all respects the reasonableness of the whole story of the White Whale, and especially of the catastrophe. For this is one of those disheartening cases where truth needs fully as much propping up as error. So ignorant are most landsmen of some of the plainest and most palpable wonders of the world that, without some hints about the plain facts, historical and otherwise, of the fishery, they might scoff at Moby Dick as a monstrous fable, or, still worse and more detestable, a hideous and intolerable allegory.

First: Though most men have some vague, flitting ideas of the general perils of the grand fishery, they have nothing like a fixed, vivid conception of those perils and of how often they recur. One reason, perhaps, is that not one in fifty of the actual disasters and accidental deaths in the fishery ever finds a public record at home, however brief and quickly forgotten that record may be. Do you suppose that that poor fellow there — who at this very moment, perhaps, caught by the whale-line off the coast of New Guinea, is being carried down to the bottom of the sea by the sounding leviathan — do you suppose that poor fellow's name will appear in the newspaper obituaries you will read tomorrow at breakfast? No: because the mails are very irregular between here and New Guinea. In fact, have you ever heard anything that could be called regular news, direct or indirect, from New Guinea? Yet I tell you that on one particular voyage I made to the Pacific, among many others we spoke — that is, hailed at sea — thirty different ships, every one of which had had a death by a whale, some of them more than one, and three that had each lost a boat's crew. For God's sake, be economical with your lamps and candles! There is not a gallon you burn that did not cost at least one drop of man's blood.

Second: People ashore have indeed some vague idea that a whale is an enormous creature of enormous power. But I have always found that when I have described to them some specific example of this twofold enormousness, they have pointedly complimented me on my facetiousness — when, I declare upon my soul, I was no more trying to be funny than Moses when he wrote the history of the plagues of Egypt.

But fortunately the particular point I am after here can be established on testimony entirely independent of my own. That point is this: the Sperm Whale is in some cases powerful enough, knowing enough, and judiciously malicious enough, with direct premeditation, to stave in, utterly destroy, and sink a large ship; and what is more, the Sperm Whale actually has done it.

First: In the year 1820 the ship Essex, Captain Pollard, of Nantucket, was cruising in the Pacific Ocean. One day she saw spouts, lowered her boats, and gave chase to a shoal of sperm whales. Before long several of the whales were wounded, when suddenly a very large whale, escaping from the boats, broke out of the shoal and bore straight down upon the ship. Dashing his forehead against her hull, he stove her in so badly that in less than "ten minutes" she settled down and fell over. Not a surviving plank of her has been seen since. After the most severe exposure, part of the crew reached land in their boats. When he had at last returned home, Captain Pollard sailed once more for the Pacific in command of another ship, but the gods shipwrecked him again on unknown rocks and breakers; for the second time his ship was utterly lost, and, at once forswearing the sea, he has never tempted it since. Captain Pollard lives in Nantucket to this day. I have seen Owen Chace, who was chief mate of the Essex at the time of the tragedy; I have read his plain and faithful narrative; I have talked with his son; and all this within a few miles of the scene of the catastrophe.*

*The following are extracts from Chace's narrative: "Every fact seemed to warrant me in concluding that it was anything but chance which directed his operations; he made two separate attacks upon the ship, at a short interval between them, both of which, according to their direction, were calculated to do us the most injury, by being made ahead, and thereby combining the speed of the two objects for the shock; to effect which, the exact maneuvers which he made were necessary. His aspect was most horrible, and such as indicated resentment and fury. He came directly from the shoal which we had just before entered, and in which we had struck three of his companions, as if fired with revenge for their sufferings." Again: "At all events, the whole circumstances taken together, all happening before my own eyes, and producing, at the time, impressions in my mind of decided, calculating mischief on the part of the whale (many of which impressions I cannot now recall), induce me to be satisfied that I am correct in my opinion."

Here are his reflections some while after leaving the ship, on a black night in an open boat, when he had almost given up hope of reaching any friendly shore. "The dark ocean and swelling waters were nothing; the fears of being swallowed up by some dreadful tempest, or dashed upon hidden rocks, with all the other ordinary subjects of fearful contemplation, seemed scarcely entitled to a moment's thought; the dismal looking wreck, and the horrid aspect and revenge of the whale, wholly engrossed my reflections, until day again made its appearance."
In another place — page 45 — he speaks of "the mysterious and mortal attack of the animal."

Second: The ship Union, also of Nantucket, was totally lost off the Azores in 1807 by a similar attack, but the authentic details of this catastrophe I have never happened to encounter, though from whale hunters I have now and then heard passing references to it.

Third: Some eighteen or twenty years ago Commodore J——, then commanding an American sloop-of-war of the first class, happened to be dining with a party of whaling captains on board a Nantucket ship in the harbor of Oahu, Sandwich Islands. When the conversation turned to whales, the Commodore was pleased to be skeptical about the amazing strength attributed to them by the professional gentlemen present. He flatly denied, for example, that any whale could strike his stout sloop-of-war hard enough to make her leak so much as a thimbleful. Very good; but there is more to come. Some weeks later the Commodore set sail in this impregnable craft for Valparaiso. But he was stopped on the way by a portly sperm whale, who asked for a few moments of confidential business with him. That business consisted of giving the Commodore's craft such a thwack that, with all his pumps going, he made straight for the nearest port to heave her down — tip her on her side — and repair her. I am not superstitious, but I consider the Commodore's interview with that whale providential. Was not Saul of Tarsus converted from unbelief by a similar fright? I tell you, the sperm whale will stand no nonsense.

I will now refer you to Langsdorff's Voyages for a small detail particularly interesting to me. Langsdorff, you should know, was attached to the Russian Admiral Krusenstern's famous Discovery Expedition at the beginning of the current century. Captain Langsdorff begins his seventeenth chapter thus:

"By the thirteenth of May our ship was ready to sail, and the next day we were out in the open sea, on our way to Ochotsh. The weather was very clear and fine, but so intolerably cold that we were obliged to keep on our fur clothing. For some days we had very little wind; it was not till the nineteenth that a brisk gale from the northwest sprang up. An uncommon large whale, the body of which was larger than the ship itself, lay almost at the surface of the water, but was not perceived by any one on board till the moment when the ship, which was in full sail, was almost upon him, so that it was impossible to prevent its striking against him. We were thus placed in the most imminent danger, as this gigantic creature, setting up its back, raised the ship three feet at least out of the water. The masts reeled, and the sails fell altogether, while we who were below all sprang instantly upon the deck, concluding that we had struck upon some rock; instead of this we saw the monster sailing off with the utmost gravity and solemnity. Captain D'Wolf applied immediately to the pumps to examine whether or not the vessel had received any damage from the shock, but we found that very happily it had escaped entirely uninjured."

Now, the Captain D'Wolf referred to here as commanding the ship in question is a New Englander who, after a long life of unusual adventures as a sea-captain, now lives in the village of Dorchester near Boston. I have the honor of being his nephew. I have questioned him particularly about this passage in Langsdorff. He confirms every word. The ship, however, was by no means a large one: a Russian craft built on the Siberian coast, and bought by my uncle after he had bartered away the vessel in which he sailed from home.

In the voyage of Lionel Wafer, one of ancient Dampier's old chums — that straightforward, manly book of old-fashioned adventure, so full of honest wonders — I found a small incident set down so like what I just quoted from Langsdorff that I cannot resist inserting it here as a supporting example, if one is needed.

Lionel, it seems, was headed for "John Ferdinando," as he calls what is now Juan Fernández. "In our way thither," he says, "about four o'clock in the morning, when we were about one hundred and fifty leagues from the Main of America, our ship felt a terrible shock, which put our men in such consternation that they could hardly tell where they were or what to think; but every one began to prepare for death. And, indeed, the shock was so sudden and violent, that we took it for granted the ship had struck against a rock; but when the amazement was a little over, we cast the lead, and sounded, but found no ground. * * * * * The suddenness of the shock made the guns leap in their carriages, and several of the men were shaken out of their hammocks. Captain Davis, who lay with his head on a gun, was thrown out of his cabin!" Lionel goes on to blame the shock on an earthquake, and seems to back up that explanation by stating that a great earthquake at roughly that time really did cause great damage along the Spanish-held mainland. But I wouldn't be very surprised if, in the darkness of that early morning hour, the shock was actually caused by an unseen whale butting the hull straight up from below.

I might go on with several more examples, known to me one way or another, of the great power and malice the sperm whale at times shows. In more than one instance he has been known not only to chase the attacking boats back to their ships, but to pursue the ship itself and hold out for a long time against all the lances hurled at him from its decks. The English ship Pusie Hall can tell a story on that score; and as for his strength, let me say that there have been cases where the lines attached to a running sperm whale have, in a calm, been transferred to the ship and made fast there, the whale towing her great hull through the water as a horse walks off with a cart. Again, it is very often observed that if the sperm whale, once struck, is given time to rally, he then acts not so often with blind rage as with willful, deliberate designs of destruction against his pursuers; and it says something eloquent about his character that, when attacked, he will often open his mouth and hold it in that dreadful gape for several minutes on end. But I must be content with only one more, concluding illustration — a remarkable and most significant one, from which you will not fail to see not only that the most marvelous event in this book is corroborated by plain facts of the present day, but that these marvels (like all marvels) are mere repetitions of the ages; so that for the millionth time we say amen with Solomon — truly, there is nothing new under the sun.

In the sixth century of the Christian era lived Procopius, a Christian magistrate of Constantinople, in the days when Justinian was Emperor and Belisarius was general. As many know, he wrote the history of his own times, a work of uncommon value in every way. By the best authorities, he has always been considered a most trustworthy and unsensational historian, except in one or two particulars that do not affect the matter I am about to mention.

Now, Procopius reports in this history of his that while he was prefect of Constantinople, a great sea-monster was caught in the nearby Propontis, or Sea of Marmora, after it had been wrecking ships in those waters, off and on, for more than fifty years. A fact recorded like this in serious history is hard to dispute, and there is no reason anyone should want to. The account does not say exactly what species the monster was. But because it destroyed ships, and for other reasons too, it must have been a whale — and I lean strongly toward a sperm whale. Let me explain why. For a long time I assumed the sperm whale had never been known in the Mediterranean or in the deep waters that connect with it. Even now I am sure those seas are not, and perhaps under the present order of things never can be, a place where he regularly gathers in herds. But recent research has shown me that in modern times the sperm whale has turned up in the Mediterranean in isolated cases. I have it on good authority that a Commodore Davis of the British navy found a sperm whale's skeleton on the Barbary coast. And since a warship passes easily through the Dardanelles, a sperm whale could take the same route out of the Mediterranean into the Propontis.

In the Propontis, as far as I can learn, none of that peculiar substance called brit — the food of the right whale — is to be found. But I have every reason to believe that the food of the sperm whale — squid or cuttlefish — lurks at the bottom of that sea, because large creatures of that sort, though by no means the largest, have been found at its surface. If, then, you properly put these statements together and reason on them a bit, you will clearly see that, according to all human reasoning, Procopius's sea-monster, which for half a century stove in the ships of a Roman Emperor, must in all probability have been a sperm whale.
